title: Week 113 · Lesson 137: Pediatric Rashes & Skin Disorders — FNP-Level Pattern Recognition and Danger-Sign Triage
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 113 — Lesson 137: Pediatric Rashes & Skin Disorders

FNP-level goal: Describe pediatric skin findings precisely, combine morphology and distribution with systemic status and exposure history, manage common inflammatory and infectious disorders safely, avoid unnecessary antimicrobials and dietary restriction, and recognize nonblanching, blistering, mucosal, rapidly progressive, or safeguarding presentations.

Learning Objectives

  • Use lesion morphology, blanching, distribution, timing, and systemic findings to build a differential.
  • Manage atopic dermatitis with barrier repair, anti-inflammatory therapy, trigger reduction, and infection assessment.
  • Distinguish impetigo, cellulitis, abscess, tinea, scabies, and common viral exanthems.
  • Recognize meningococcal disease, Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, and anaphylaxis.
  • Identify bruising, burns, patterned injury, or history-examination mismatch requiring safeguarding action.

Part 1 — The Sick Child With a Rash

Begin with appearance, airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, fever, pain, hydration, and progression. A rash is an emergency when accompanied by shock, respiratory compromise, facial or tongue swelling, altered consciousness, toxic appearance, rapidly spreading purpura, extensive blistering or skin pain, mucosal erosion, or severe dehydration.

Do not spend the first minutes naming lesions in an unstable child. Stabilize, isolate when indicated, and escalate.

Part 2 — Describe Before Diagnosing

Document primary morphology: macule, papule, plaque, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal, nodule, petechia, purpura, erosion, ulcer, crust, or scale. Note color, size, borders, blanching, tenderness, warmth, fluctuance, and secondary changes. Distribution may be flexural, extensor, dermatomal, acral, palmoplantar, perioral, diaper, intertriginous, or generalized.

Ask which lesion appeared first and how it evolved. Photos from earlier stages may be useful. Medication timing, fever relationship, vaccines, travel, contacts, pets, insects, new products, foods, immune status, and family history change the differential.

Part 3 — Atopic Dermatitis Is a Barrier and Inflammation Disorder

Atopic dermatitis produces chronic or relapsing pruritic inflammation with age-dependent distribution. Infants often have facial and extensor involvement; older children more often have flexural disease. Itch, sleep disruption, excoriation, lichenification, pigment change, and family atopy support the diagnosis.

Core care includes regular fragrance-free moisturizer, gentle bathing and cleansing, avoidance of proven irritants, and topical anti-inflammatory therapy matched to age, site, severity, formulation, and duration. Teach fingertip-unit or other clear quantity guidance and demonstrate where treatment goes. Steroid fear can cause undertreatment; unmonitored high-potency use on thin skin can cause harm.

Part 4 — Eczema Maintenance and Escalation

Use proactive intermittent therapy on recurrent sites when appropriate and consider nonsteroidal topical agents according to age and indication. Wet-wrap therapy can help selected severe flares with instruction. The 2026 AAD pediatric guideline continues to support moisturizing care and evidence-based topical therapies while discouraging routine topical antimicrobials and unsupported broad dietary or environmental interventions.

Refer or collaborate when diagnosis is uncertain, disease is severe or refractory, sleep and quality of life are substantially impaired, recurrent infection occurs, systemic treatment is considered, or contact dermatitis needs testing.

Part 5 — Infection in Eczema

Honey crust, pustules, weeping, focal pain, rapidly worsening erythema, fever, or cellulitis may indicate bacterial superinfection. Grouped painful vesicles, punched-out erosions, fever, and malaise raise concern for eczema herpeticum, which requires urgent antiviral evaluation and eye assessment when facial involvement is present.

Do not label every wet flare infected or prescribe routine topical antibiotics. Culture is useful for recurrent, severe, unusual, or treatment-resistant infection.

Part 6 — Impetigo, Cellulitis, and Abscess

Nonbullous impetigo often begins as papules or pustules that rupture into honey-colored crust. Limited disease may be treated topically, while numerous lesions or outbreak circumstances may require oral therapy targeting likely group A strep and Staphylococcus aureus under current local guidance.

Cellulitis causes spreading warmth, erythema, swelling, and tenderness without a drainable center. Abscess produces a focal collection that may be fluctuant; source control is central. Marking margins can help monitor selected cellulitis. Rapid progression, pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, anesthesia, systemic toxicity, or shock raises concern for necrotizing infection and requires emergency surgery-oriented evaluation.

Part 7 — Tinea and Scabies

Tinea corporis often forms an annular scaly plaque with an active border; tinea capitis may cause scale, alopecia, broken hairs, lymphadenopathy, or inflammatory kerion and generally requires systemic therapy because topical agents do not penetrate the hair shaft adequately. Confirm uncertain disease with appropriate microscopy or culture rather than adding steroids to every ring-shaped rash.

Scabies causes intense itch, often worse at night, with burrows or papules on wrists, finger webs, waist, axillae, genital areas, or broader infant distribution. Treat the patient and relevant close contacts simultaneously, follow product age and safety guidance, clean or isolate appropriate items, and explain that itch can persist after successful treatment.

Part 8 — Diaper Dermatitis

Irritant diaper dermatitis affects convex surfaces and often spares deep folds. Candida commonly involves folds with satellite papules or pustules. Consider bacterial infection, psoriasis, nutritional deficiency, immunodeficiency, or neglect when severe, persistent, erosive, or atypical.

Frequent changes, gentle cleansing, air exposure, and thick barrier ointment are foundational. Target antifungal or antibacterial therapy to a supported diagnosis.

Part 9 — Viral Exanthems

Integrate the order of fever and rash, vaccination, exposures, oral findings, palms and soles, and systemic status. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease can produce oral ulcers and acral lesions; roseola classically brings rash as fever resolves; parvovirus can cause slapped-cheek and lacy rash; varicella has lesions in different stages.

Measles remains a public-health concern. Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and descending rash in an exposed or underimmunized child requires immediate masking, isolation, public-health coordination, and testing—not waiting in a common reception area.

Part 10 — Petechiae and Purpura

Petechiae do not blanch. Local petechiae above the nipple line after forceful vomiting may be mechanical, but fever, toxic appearance, rapid spread, shock, neck stiffness, or widespread purpura raises concern for invasive infection or coagulopathy. Also consider platelet disorders, vasculitis, leukemia, trauma, and abuse.

Palpable purpura on the legs or buttocks with abdominal or joint pain suggests IgA vasculitis and requires blood pressure, urinalysis, renal follow-up, and abdominal emergency assessment. Do not reassure based on the rash alone.

Part 11 — Urticaria and Anaphylaxis

Urticaria produces transient raised pruritic wheals that migrate and resolve without bruising. Viral illness is a common trigger in children; food or medication allergy is considered from timing and reproducibility. Individual lesions lasting more than 24 hours, pain, bruising, fever, or systemic symptoms suggest another diagnosis.

Urticaria plus respiratory compromise, hypotension, repetitive vomiting, or involvement of multiple organ systems after a likely exposure may be anaphylaxis. Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line; antihistamines do not treat airway obstruction or shock. Arrange emergency monitoring and prescribe an action plan and autoinjector when indicated.

Part 12 — Blistering and Mucosal Emergencies

Skin pain, dusky targetoid lesions, blistering, epidermal detachment, and ocular, oral, or genital mucosal erosions after medication or infection raises concern for Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Tender widespread erythema and superficial peeling in a young child may suggest staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

These are hospital emergencies involving fluid, infection, pain, eye, airway, and medication management. Stop suspected culprit medication when clinically appropriate and escalate immediately.

Part 13 — Safeguarding

Consider developmental ability, location, pattern, symmetry, and explanation for bruises or burns. Bruising in a nonmobile infant, patterned marks, immersion lines, genital injury, multiple injury stages, or history inconsistent with development requires child-protection evaluation. Document objective description and body location; avoid accusatory or leading language.

Clinical Case 1 — Eczema or Infection?

A six-year-old with eczema develops fever, painful clustered vesicles, and punched-out facial erosions. The FNP recognizes possible eczema herpeticum and arranges urgent antiviral and ocular evaluation rather than increasing topical steroid alone.

Clinical Case 2 — Fever and Nonblanching Rash

A three-year-old has fever, lethargy, delayed capillary refill, and rapidly spreading purpura. The FNP initiates emergency sepsis care and transfer; the rash is not observed at home for evolution.

Clinical Case 3 — Ring-Shaped Treatment Failure

A school-age child has an enlarging annular scaly plaque after a combination steroid cream. The FNP considers tinea incognito, confirms fungal disease when needed, stops inappropriate steroid exposure, and uses site-appropriate antifungal therapy.

FNP High-Yield Framework: SKIN

  1. S — Stability and systemic symptoms: shock, airway, fever, pain, mucosa, rapid progression.
  2. K — Know the lesion: morphology, blanching, distribution, first lesion, evolution.
  3. I — Identify mechanism: inflammatory, infectious, allergic, vascular, drug, traumatic.
  4. N — Name treatment and next step: barrier care, targeted antimicrobial, emergency escalation, follow-up.

Take-Home Summary

Pediatric rashes become manageable when described before labeled. Barrier repair and anti-inflammatory care anchor eczema treatment; targeted therapy replaces reflex antimicrobials; and systemic illness, nonblanching progression, severe pain, mucosal disease, blistering, anaphylaxis, or suspicious injury demands immediate escalation.

Educational note: Follow current AAD pediatric dermatitis, CDC infectious-disease, local antimicrobial, public-health, allergy, and child-protection guidance. Shock, airway symptoms, rapidly progressive purpura, extensive blistering, mucosal erosion, severe pain, necrotizing signs, or concerning injury requires urgent care.
